title: Review: Circulatory systems and blood vessels; Plant transport: xylem and transpiration; Limiting factors and rate of photosynthesis; Human gas exchange and ventilation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX05#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX02a#t4 term and clue written for the game; EX02a#t2 term and clue written for the game; EX05#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX02a#N.6, EX05#N.8, EX10a#N.2, EX10b#N.10a, PS04#N.3, EX02a#N.11, EX05#N.17, EX10a#N.7, PS04#N.8, EX05#N.18, EX10a#N.12a, EX05#N.11. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Vasoconstriction
items.clue: The contracting of smooth muscle in an arteriole wall

items.label: Internal intercostal muscles
items.clue: Contract only in forced breathing out, pulling the ribs down and in

items.label: Surfactant
items.clue: Substance in the moist lining of the air sacs that stops them collapsing

items.label: Endothelium
items.clue: Smooth inner lining of a blood vessel, one flat cell thick, causing little friction

questions.stem: Mammalian lungs contain a branched network of bronchioles ending in millions of alveoli. How does this branching contribute to gas exchange?

options.text: It multiplies the area of airway wall across which gases are exchanged into the blood as air travels inward.
It packs a very large alveolar surface, each part close to a capillary bed, into the volume of the thorax.
It lets the lungs grow larger, and a larger organ must have a bigger surface for gas exchange.
It houses the muscle that contracts to pump air in and out of the alveoli found at the end of every branch.

questions.stem: What is the role of the elastic tissue in the wall of an artery?

options.text: It contracts in waves behind the blood to push it along the artery towards the tissues.
It makes the wall stiff and rigid so that the high pressure cannot burst the artery.
It stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure.
It forms flaps that actively open and shut to push blood forwards along the artery.

questions.explanation: Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy; recoil returns it while the ventricle relaxes, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.

questions.stem: Why is transpiration described as a consequence of gas exchange rather than as a process the leaf carries out for its own sake?

options.text: The plant opens its stomata in order to lose water, because transpiration is needed to pull water up through the xylem.
Stomata must be open for carbon dioxide to enter, and water vapour inevitably diffuses out through the same pores.
Water vapour escapes across the cuticle and epidermis wherever gases are exchanged over the leaf surface.
Transpiration is evaporation that depends only on temperature, so it happens whether or not the stomata are open.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, which can only enter through open stomata. While they are open, water vapour from the saturated air spaces diffuses out down its concentration gradient to the drier atmosphere; the water loss is an unavoidable side effect of gas exchange.

questions.stem: A grower's greenhouse plants wilt on hot afternoons. The grower wants to slow their transpiration. Which change would do this?

options.text: Switch on fans to blow air over the leaves, because cooler leaves lose less water.
Water the soil more, so that the plants no longer need to transpire as much.
Dry the greenhouse air, because humid air keeps the leaves wet and speeds water loss.
Mist the air to raise the humidity, so the water-vapour gradient is smaller.

questions.explanation: Less difference between the air spaces and the air means slower diffusion of water vapour out of the stomata.

questions.stem: Pondweed submerged in water at 25 °C with the carbon dioxide concentration of ordinary air was exposed to increasing light intensity. The rate of photosynthesis rose at first and then levelled off, staying constant however much the light intensity was increased. Which change is most likely to raise the rate at this plateau?

options.text: Moving the lamp even closer, so that the light intensity becomes higher still.
Adding sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water to raise the carbon dioxide concentration.
Nothing, because the plateau is the maximum rate of which the plant is capable.
Adding more water to the beaker, since water is a reactant in photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?

options.text: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.
The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move up so that air is drawn in to fill the space.

questions.explanation: Larger thorax volume, pressure in the lungs below atmospheric, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.

questions.stem: In a section, vessel P has a wall 0.30 mm thick around a round lumen 0.40 mm across. Vessel Q has a wall 0.10 mm thick around a flattened lumen 1.6 mm across. Which identification is correct?

options.text: P is a vein: it needs a thick muscular wall to pump blood back to the heart.
Neither can be identified, because a section cannot show whether the blood is oxygenated.
Q is an artery: its wide lumen carries the most blood at high pressure.
P is an artery and Q is a vein: compare wall thickness with lumen width.

questions.explanation: P's wall is thick relative to its lumen (0.30 : 0.40); Q's is thin relative to its lumen (0.10 : 1.6).

questions.stem: Why are the walls of xylem vessels thickened with lignin?

options.text: To seal the vessel completely so that no water can escape through the side walls into surrounding cells.
To provide the mitochondria and cytoplasm of the vessel with a surface on which to generate ATP for transport.
To hold the plant upright, which is the only function that lignin has anywhere in the xylem.
To withstand the tension in the water column so that the vessel is not pulled inwards and collapsed.

questions.explanation: The negative pressure potential generated by transpiration would suck a soft-walled tube flat. Lignified walls are rigid enough to withstand these tensions, keeping the vessel open for unimpeded flow; they also contribute to supporting the plant.

questions.stem: A student places a lamp at different distances from a beaker of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution kept at 25 °C, and counts the bubbles of gas released per minute at each distance. Which correctly identifies the variables?

options.text: Independent: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: bubbles per minute; dependent: distance of lamp
Controlled variable: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: temperature of 25 °C; dependent: bubbles per minute

questions.explanation: Lamp distance is deliberately changed (it sets light intensity): independent. Bubble count is measured: dependent. Temperature and hydrogencarbonate concentration are controlled.

questions.stem: With age, the walls of large arteries lose elastic tissue and become stiffer. Blood pressure in an arm artery is measured at its highest (as the ventricle contracts) and its lowest (between beats). What change in these readings is expected?

options.text: The readings become steadier, because a stiff wall resists the surges better than a stretchy one.
The highest reading rises and the lowest falls: the swing in pressure gets bigger.
The lowest reading falls to zero, because nothing keeps blood under pressure between beats.
No change, because the muscle in the artery wall contracts with each beat to keep the pressure steady.

questions.stem: Florists cut the stems of fresh flowers under water. A stem cut in air and then put in a vase often wilts, even though its cut end is in water. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Cutting the stem removes the roots, which were pumping water up to the flowers, so the flow stops.
Water in the xylem is under positive pressure, so it pours out of the cut end and the stem empties.
Cutting kills the xylem cells, so they can no longer use ATP to move water up the stem.
Xylem water is under tension, so air is drawn into the cut vessels and breaks the columns.

questions.stem: A muscle receives blood through a network of thousands of capillaries rather than through a single vessel of the same total volume. What is the advantage of this arrangement for exchange?

options.text: A single wide vessel would have more wall area than thousands of narrow ones, so exchange inside it would be faster.
The narrow capillaries force the blood through faster, so more oxygen is delivered to the muscle each second.
Each capillary has fenestrations, which are needed so that cells can pass out of the blood into the muscle.
The total surface area of the many narrow, branching vessels is far larger, and all the blood is close to a wall.
